title: Hold every hour
hookLine: take hold of each hour, Seneca begins, and you'll depend less on tomorrow

cards: Open the screen-time report on your phone and it will tell you, to the minute, where your week went. Plenty of people look once, wince, and never open it again. Seneca didn't have the report.
He had something like it in his own head, and in the very first letter to Lucilius he opens it and makes himself look. The first lesson of a hundred twenty-four isn't about God or virtue.
It's about time, and where ours keeps going.

teach.b: Letter one begins, in Latin, vindica te tibi: claim yourself for yourself. Vindica is a legal word, used for claiming property, or claiming a person's freedom in court.
Seneca is telling Lucilius to take himself back, the way you'd take back something taken from you. Then the three thieves.
Some of our time, he says, is torn away from us, some is quietly stolen, and some just slips through our fingers. The most shameful loss comes from carelessness.
Most of life passes doing the wrong thing, much of it doing nothing, and all of it doing something other than what we meant to. Then the line that names this day.

teach.h: HOLD EVERY HOUR IN YOUR GRASP.
teach.b: In Gummere's translation: hold every hour in your grasp. Take hold of today's work, Seneca says, and you'll depend less on tomorrow's. Year one gave us the sentence that follows soon after: nothing is ours except time.
And Seneca doesn't pretend he's mastered it.

He keeps accounts of his own time, he tells Lucilius, the way someone free-handed but careful keeps a household budget. He can't boast that he wastes nothing, but he can say what he's wasting, and why.
He's not preaching from a mountaintop. He's a man in his sixties, honest about his losses, and starting today.
That's what holding an hour looks like: not a perfect schedule, just taking the next one in your hand.

how: Readers of Seneca often keep a simple account of their time, noticing where the day went in the evening, and try to give each hour a purpose before it begins.

s: Seneca's first letter is mainly about the gods
it's about time: claiming it back and holding each hour. death comes up only as part of that.
vindica is a legal word for claiming property or freedom
Seneca tells Lucilius to claim himself back, as if in court.
Seneca claims he never wastes time
he admits losses; he only says he can account for where it went.

games.q: you're Lucilius. your old friend writes that you're letting your time be stolen. what's the first thing he tells you to do?
o: claim yourself back and hold every hour.
games.why: letter one opens with vindica te tibi, claim yourself for yourself, and then: hold every hour in your grasp.

practice: Look at the clock and think about the next hour, the real one, not the ideal one, and pick one thing it's for: the report, the walk, the meal with your family, sleep.
Picture the thief that usually shows up, the scroll, the side errand, the drift, and decide now what you'll do when it knocks. Hold the hour in your hand before it starts.

wordCard.voice: Three thieves, Seneca says, take your time: some torn away, some stolen quietly, some just slipping through carelessness. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: claim yourself for yourself, the first words of advice in Seneca's first letter.

carryVoice: Your line: hold this hour. Torn away, stolen or slipped: not this one. Day four hundred thirty-two.
